power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: Early defibrillation is the principal modifiable determinant of survival after shockable out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, but studies restricted to defibrillated patients cannot observe those who had degenerated before a responder arrived.
We quantified this loss and its population-level consequences.
Methods: We analysed 368,496 bystander-witnessed adult arrests of presumed cardiac origin in the All-Japan Utstein Registry (2005-2024).
Modified Poisson models with marginal standardization estimated the proportion with a shockable rhythm at emergency medical services (EMS) contact and 1-month survival as functions of elapsed time.
Assuming exchangeability within strata of bystander category and age, we estimated the additional survivors had patients reached at ≥15 minutes been reached at 5-10 minutes.

Results: The adjusted proportion with a shockable rhythm was 33.1% (95% CI, 30.2-36.5) at 1 minute, 24.7% (24.4-24.9) at 9 minutes and 8.4% (8.0-8.8) at 30 minutes, a relative decline of 4.8% per minute between 5 and 30 minutes.

Adjusted 1-month survival fell from 39.5% (38.4-40.6) at 9 minutes to 15.9% (15.1-16.7) at 20 minutes after EMS defibrillation, and from 63.5% (59.9-67.3) at 3 minutes to 47.2% (44.4-50.0) at 10 minutes after bystander defibrillation; each minute cost 2.1 to 2.7 percentage points in both pathways.

Shifting the 119,982 patients reached at ≥15 minutes to 5-10 minutes yielded 6,465 additional survivors (6,259-6,669) over 20 years (323 per year; number needed to treat, 18.6), 59.1% through rhythm preservation.
Familywitnessed arrests and the "other" bystander category, predominantly institutional, accounted for 77.4%.

Conclusions: The proportion of patients shockable at EMS contact was approximately 5% lower for each additional minute after collapse, and survival fell by about two percentage points per 53 minute whoever delivered the shock.

Under the model's assumptions, most of the benefit of 54 faster contact derives from reaching patients while still shockable, chiefly in arrests witnessed by 55 family members or in institutional settings.

Second, if the interval from collapse to first responder contact were shortened at a population level, how much of the resulting benefit would arise from each of these two mechanisms, and how large would the total be.

Using a nationwide, population-based registry covering 20 years of OHCA in Japan, we estimated the rate at which shockable rhythms are lost with elapsed time, characterized the relationship between the interval to first defibrillation and survival, and translated these observed relationships into population-level counterfactual scenarios in which first contact occurred earlier than observed.

We conducted a nationwide, population-based observational cohort study using the All-Japan Utstein Registry, a prospective registry of OHCA maintained by the Fire and Disaster Management Agency of Japan, covering all arrests attended by emergency medical services (EMS) nationwide according to standardized Utstein-style definitions. 9 Records from 1 January 2005 through 31December 2024 were analyzed.

text.text: Exact duplicate records (n=210) were removed, and 18 records filed in the 2005 registry file whose year field was coded as 2004, all with event dates in 2005, were assigned to 2005.
The study follows the STROBE reporting guideline.
We identified witnessed arrests of presumed cardiac origin in adults aged 18 years or older.
The registry classifies bystanders as family members, friends, colleagues, passers-by or other.
Two further exclusions were applied on the basis of the recorded event sequence.

Early defibrillation is the single most time-critical intervention in the management of out-ofhospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) caused by a shockable rhythm. 1 Nationwide dissemination of public-access automated external defibrillators in Japan has been accompanied by an increase in the proportion of patients receiving a bystander shock and by improved neurologically favorable survival at the population level. 2, 3 The underlying rationale is that survival after ventricular fibrillation declines rapidly from the moment of collapse, and that shortening the interval to the first shock is therefore the principal modifiable determinant of outcome. 4, 5, 6 Most evidence supporting this rationale, however, has been generated from studies defined by the receipt of defibrillation.

First, we excluded arrests witnessed by fire department or EMS personnel, in whom EMS contact preceded or coincided with the recorded witness time in 96.8%, because the time structure of resuscitation differs fundamentally (Supplementary Methods S2).

Second, we excluded patients in whom the emergency call preceded the witnessed collapse, indicating that EMS had already been activated for another reason; in these patients the interval from collapse to contact is mechanically shortened (Supplementary Methods S3).
All eligible patients were included; no sample size calculation was performed.
Timestamps were assessed independently, without assuming which of two inconsistent timestamps was erroneous.
Witness times were classified by calendar consistency against the EMS contact time, and defibrillation recorded after hospital arrival was treated as logically inconsistent.
Problematic timestamps were set to missing, with one exception: because every analysis depends on the time of collapse, patients were excluded (Supplementary Methods S1).
The bystander automated external defibrillator fields changed in 2021.

Before 2021, bystander defibrillation was a binary indicator whose accompanying timestamp did not record the shock: the timestamp's prevalence tracked that of bystander chest compression to within 1.2 percentage points between 2005 and 2012.
From 2021 a four-level field was accompanied by a timestamp of shock delivery.

Across the change the proportion receiving bystander defibrillation was continuous, but the recorded interval from collapse shifted 3 to 5 minutes later at every quantile with no change in survival, so the bystander-pathway analysis was restricted to 2021-2024.
The EMS defibrillation timestamp was stable throughout (median 14 minutes in both periods) and was analyzed for the full period (Supplementary Methods S4).

For the rhythm-decay analysis the exposure was the interval from collapse to EMS contact, when the rhythm is first documented, among patients reached within 40 minutes who had not received a bystander shock and in whom ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity or asystole was documented.
The population-level analysis used the same interval and does not depend on either defibrillation timestamp.
The primary outcome was 1-month survival; the secondary outcome was a favorable neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 1 or 2) at 1 month.

The two delivery pathways occupied almost non-overlapping exposure ranges and served different populations, so separate models were fitted over each pathway's range of support: 0-15 minutes for bystander defibrillation (2021-2024) and 9-40 minutes for EMS defibrillation (2005-2024).
The EMS lower bound of 9 minutes was chosen because, after exclusion of callbefore-collapse cases, shorter intervals comprised a heavily selected residual (Supplementary Methods S3).

Within each pathway, 1-month survival was modeled by modified Poisson regression with a log link, 11 with elapsed time modeled as a restricted cubic spline and, for the bystander pathway, a separate indicator for shocks recorded at zero minutes.

text.text: After standardization, the adjusted proportion fell from 33.1% (95% CI, 30.2-36.5) at 1 minute, where data were sparse, to 28.6% (28.0-29.1) at 5 minutes, 24.7% (24.4-24.9) at 9 minutes, 18.0% (17.7-18.2) at 15 minutes, 13.4% (13.1-13.7) at 20 minutes, and 8.4% (8.0-8.8) at 30 minutes, corresponding to a relative decline of approximately 4.8% per minute between 5 and 30 minutes.
The rate of decline differed by bystander category (P for interaction <0.001).

text.text: At 9 minutes, the proportion with a shockable rhythm standardized to age 78 years was 27.9% for colleaguewitnessed and 27.4% for friend-witnessed arrests, compared with 20.5% for family-witnessed and 17.9% for the "other" category, which predominantly comprised institutional settings (Supplementary Figure S1).

text.text: The bystander pathway (2021-2024) comprised 4,270 patients and the EMS pathway (2005-2024) 76,748.

The two pathways served markedly different populations (Table 1): bystanderdefibrillated patients were less often witnessed by a family member (7.4% versus 65.2%), more often in the "other" category (43.0% versus 13.4%), and almost universally received bystander chest compressions (98.6% versus 56.3%).

text.text: Median time to first defibrillation was 5 minutes (IQR 2-8) and 14 minutes (IQR 11-19), respectively.
One-month survival was 54.2% and 25.1%, and favorable neurological outcome 45.6% and 15.7%.
Adjusted, marginally standardized survival declined steeply with elapsed time in both pathways (Figure 3).
text.formatted: Adjusted, marginally standardized survival declined steeply with elapsed time in both pathways (Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>).

text.text: In the bystander pathway, survival was highest within the first 4 minutes (63.5% at 3 minutes; 95% CI, 59.8-67.7) and fell to 57.3% (54.7-60.0) at 5 minutes, 47.0% (44.2-49.8) at 10 minutes and 34.3% (28.5-39.4) at 14 minutes, a relative decline of 5.5% per minute between 3 and 14 minutes.
Survival at 0 minutes was 49.9% (44.7-55.3), lower than at 1-4 minutes.

In the EMS pathway, survival fell from 39.3% (38.3-40.4) at 9 minutes to 31.1% (30.5-31.7) at 12 minutes, 23.8% (23.2-24.4) at 15 minutes, 15.7% (15.1-16.5) at 20 minutes and 6.6% (6.0-7.2) at 30 minutes, a relative decline of 8.0% per minute between 9 and 20 minutes.

Where both pathways had data (9-14 minutes), survival after bystander defibrillation exceeded survival after EMS defibrillation by 8.3 to 10.6 percentage points, with non-overlapping confidence intervals at every minute (49.8% versus 39.3% at 9 minutes; 47.0% versus 36.5% at 10 minutes; 40.6% versus 31.1% at 12 minutes; 34.3% versus 26.0% at 14 minutes).

Restricting the EMS analysis to 2021-2024 to match the bystander period narrowed the difference from 10.8 percentage points at 9 minutes to 6.8 at 14 minutes, with non-overlapping confidence intervals through 13 minutes.

Under the primary counterfactual scenario, in which the 119,982 patients reached by EMS at 15 minutes or later had instead been reached at 5-10 minutes, we estimated 6,465 additional 1month survivors (95% CI, 6,259-6,669) over the 20-year period, or 323 per year, corresponding to an NNT of 18.6 (Figure 4).

text.text: The rhythm-preservation channel accounted for 3,821 additional survivors (3,690-3,953, 59.1%), compared with 2,644 (2,511-2,776, 40.9%) from earlier defibrillation among patients already in a shockable rhythm.
Rhythm preservation accounted for the majority of the benefit in every scenario examined (54.3% to 67.7%; Supplementary Table S4).
text.formatted: Rhythm preservation accounted for the majority of the benefit in every scenario examined (54.3% to 67.7%; Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Family-witnessed arrests accounted for 3,895 additional survivors (60.2% of the total) and the "other" category for 1,107 (17.1%), together representing 77.4% of the estimated benefit.

Repeating the analysis with a favorable neurological outcome as the endpoint yielded 4,835 additional patients with Cerebral Performance Category 1 or 2 (4,661-5,009; 242 per year; NNT, 24.8), equivalent to 74.8% of the additional survivors, of which rhythm preservation accounted for 55.9%.
The direction of findings was consistent across scenarios (Figure 4B and Supplementary Table S4).

text.text: A more conservative target of 10-15 minutes yielded 3,452 additional survivors (3,291-3,612; 173 per year; NNT 34.8).

Restricting the target population to the 55,028 patients reached at 20 minutes or later yielded 3,361 (3,265-3,459; 168 per year) with the most favorable efficiency (16.4) and the highest contribution from rhythm preservation (67.7%).
Omitting the age stratification raised the primary estimate to 7,890 (7,657-8,122; 15.2).

Excluding patients who received bystander defibrillation, in whom the rhythm at EMS contact is a post-treatment variable, gave 6,368 (6,173-6,566; 18.1), and retaining patients in whom the call preceded the collapse gave 5,280 (5,107-5,457; 23.2).

In this nationwide study of 368,496 bystander-witnessed adult arrests over 20 years, the proportion of patients shockable at EMS contact was approximately 4.8% lower in relative terms for each additional minute after collapse, and survival after defibrillation fell by 2.1 to 2.7 percentage points per minute whoever delivered the shock.

Shifting the 119,982 patients reached at 15 minutes or later to 5-10 minutes would have yielded an estimated 6,465 additional 1-month survivors, or 323 per year (NNT, 18.6), three-fifths of them through reaching patients while they were still shockable.
The decomposition of the counterfactual into two channels is the principal contribution of this analysis.
Conventional framing of early defibrillation emphasizes the time-dependent decline in the success of a shock once delivered.
Our data indicate that this mechanism accounts for approximately two-fifths of the potential population benefit.

The remainder reflects patients who, by the time the first responder arrived, had already degenerated from a shockable to a nonshockable rhythm and therefore never became candidates for defibrillation at all.

These patients are invisible to any study restricted to defibrillation recipients. 3, 7 This allocation rests on a monotonicity assumption, that patients in a shockable rhythm when reached late would also have been shockable if reached earlier; an alternative algebraic partition of the same total would assign 23.2% rather than 59.1% to rhythm preservation (Supplementary Methods S7).

The time-dependent fall in first-shock success that constitutes Channel A has been demonstrated directly with defibrillator recordings, each additional minute of delay being associated with a 6% higher probability of failure to terminate ventricular fibrillation. 8 That analysis was restricted to patients presenting with ventricular fibrillation as the initial rhythm, a design that measures Channel A with far greater physiological precision than a registry can but that by construction cannot observe Channel B, because patients who had already left the shockable state before any rhythm was recorded are absent from its population.

text.text: The component that analysis could not observe is, under the monotonicity assumption, the larger of the two.

The share attributable to rhythm preservation rose as fewer patients remained eligible: it was lowest for colleague-witnessed arrests (48.1%), in which 34.9% of patients remained shockable at late contact compared with 12.3% of family-witnessed arrests, and highest when the target population was restricted to patients reached at 20 minutes or later (67.7%).
Because Channel A is proportional to the fraction still shockable at late contact, this gradient partly reflects the structure of the decomposition.

Earlier analyses of this registry linked the dissemination of public-access defibrillation to improved population-level neurological survival without defining an individual time origin, 2, 3 and a recent analysis matched on the timing of public-access defibrillation among recipients with ventricular fibrillation in public locations. 7 Our analysis adds residential and institutional arrests, quantifies the loss of defibrillation eligibility directly, and extends the observed relationships to a population-level counterfactual (Supplementary Table S2).

Although the per-patient benefit of earlier defibrillation was greatest in workplace and public settings, 77.4% of the estimated population benefit arose from family-witnessed arrests (60.2%) and arrests in the "other" category (17.1%), because these settings account for most cases.

Current public-access defibrillation policy in Japan has concentrated devices in transport hubs, schools and commercial premises, consistent with randomized and observational evidence of . benefit in public locations. 17, 18 Our findings indicate that the largest remaining opportunity lies in the settings that these bystander categories predominantly represent, residences and institutions, where response intervals are longest and the loss of defibrillation eligibility before first contact is correspondingly greatest; dispatch of nearby lay responders is one means of shortening this interval. 19, 20 The annual size of the target population grew from 5,385 (2005-2019 average) to 6,212 (2015-2019) and 7,843 (2020-2024; Supplementary Figure S4), and the expected annual benefit from 307 to 353 and 382 additional survivors, while the NNT rose modestly from 17.5 to 20.5.

The bystander-pathway estimates, confined to 2021-2024, are less precise.
The rhythm-decay curve is cross-sectional: it compares different patients observed at different intervals rather than tracking individual patients over time.

Among patients defibrillated by EMS, the proportion with a shockable rhythm at EMS contact fell from 94.8% at 9-11 minutes to 27.0% at 26-40 minutes (Supplementary Table S5), indicating that late defibrillations increasingly represent arrhythmia arising during resuscitation rather than delayed treatment of a persistent shockable rhythm; estimates beyond 25 minutes are not interpreted.

text.text: In the bystander pathway, survival at zero minutes was 14 percentage points below that at 3 minutes.

Patients shocked at zero minutes were older than those shocked at 1-4 minutes (median, 70 versus 66 years) and more often in the "other" category (58.0% versus 49.0%), consistent with residual confounding by institutional setting and frailty among patients . for whom a device was already in place.

Finally, the counterfactual assumes that a 5-10 minute contact interval is attainable for all patients currently reached later, which is not realistic in rural areas; the more conservative 10-15 minute scenario, yielding 173 additional survivors per year, may better represent what is operationally achievable.
Generalizability to EMS systems with different response intervals, dispatch practices or termination-of-resuscitation rules is uncertain.

Among bystander-witnessed cardiac arrests of presumed cardiac origin in Japan, the proportion of patients in a shockable rhythm at EMS contact was approximately 5% lower in relative terms for each additional minute after collapse, and survival after defibrillation fell by roughly two percentage points per minute whoever delivered the shock.

Advancing first contact from 15 minutes or more to 5-10 minutes would be expected to produce approximately 320 additional survivors per year nationally, with the majority of that benefit deriving from the preservation of defibrillation eligibility rather than from earlier delivery of a shock to patients already eligible.
Judged by bystander category, the largest remaining opportunity lies in residential and institutional settings.
